c: Barnabas

Barnabas is presented in Acts as a model Christian leader. A native of Cyprus, Barnabas was active in the Jerusalem church and demonstrated unselfish generosity in meeting the needs of the poorer members of that community (
). His given name was Joseph, but he was nicknamed Barnabas (“Son of Encouragement,”
), which indicates his character. He was a suitable person to give a fair and open-minded assessment of the new work in Antioch (
). Barnabas perceived God’s blessing there and “encouraged the believers to stay true to the Lord” (
). His sterling character was clear in his transparent goodness, abundant faith, and Spirit-filled life and work (
). The Holy Spirit chose Barnabas and Saul for a special work (known to us as the first missionary journey), and they were sent out by the church at Antioch (
Barnabas’s wisdom is evidenced in his earlier trip to Tarsus to find Saul (

). Barnabas had been impressed by the boldness of Saul’s preaching as a new Christian in Damascus and had taken him to the apostles, providing a vital introduction for a man who was under suspicion for his previous unrelenting attacks against believers. Through Barnabas’s intervention, Saul obtained needed contact with the original apostles, received their acceptance, and preached fearlessly in Jerusalem until he was forced out of the city (
). Barnabas’s trip was successful, and for a full year the two worked together in the Antioch church, drawing large crowds (
Barnabas was an impressive figure (note his reception in Lystra as Zeus,
). He was John Mark’s cousin and mentor and played a major role in giving John Mark a second chance to make good as a Christian leader after he had abandoned an earlier mission (
Barnabas knew peer pressure, and he gave in to it on one occasion even though he knew better (
). Barnabas wasn’t perfect, but he was a “Son of Encouragement,” to many and a generous, unselfish man who fostered growth in others and in the church.

Persecution
Persecution is a common experience of God’s people. God’s servants have often faced hostility and opposition (e.g.,
). Jesus himself dealt with persecution (
). At the end of his earthly life, he endured mocking, beating, and a horrible death by crucifixion, and he told his disciples to expect the same kind of treatment (
). He prepared his followers for such occasions, telling them that the Holy Spirit would give them the needed courage (

The book of Acts documents the persecution of the earliest Christians, beginning with the hostility of the Jewish high council and the attacks of Saul of Tarsus on the early church prior to his encounter with Jesus near Damascus (
; see
). Peter, John, Stephen, James, Paul, and Barnabas all suffered persecution (
). Jesus, in his parable of the farmer and the seed, noted the withering effects of persecution on those with shallow faith (

). Persecution purifies God’s people and gives them the opportunity to conform more closely to the character of Jesus. The apostles’ experiences in Acts bear out Paul’s general statement: “Everyone who wants to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (

Jesus told his disciples to expect to defend their faith in hostile settings (
), and the apostles and other leaders did so with courage and boldness (e.g.,
). Christians are called to defend their faith courageously and graciously, explaining their convictions to those who ask questions (

). Acts records frequent times of persecution (
), but Acts also reiterates that the Holy Spirit empowers disciples to bear witness in such circumstances (
). The boldness of Peter and John before the hostile high council exemplifies facing persecution with courage and power (
